title: Four readers. Four independent paths.
intent: Keep the approved UI. Organize the content around the question each reader brings.

navigation.entry: All four audience regions are visible on one sheet.
navigation.order: Read the numbered content within a region. Pan and zoom to inspect it; no page turns or hidden sections.
navigation.ending: Each region has its own conclusion. Moving the view never opens another page.
navigation.address: The sheet URL preserves its center (x, y) and zoom (z).

shared.appearance: Keep the approved visual language. User: illustrated journeys. Investor: Canton demo storyboards. Architecture: engineering diagrams. Implementation: production source only.
shared.evidence: Cite original passages beside the relevant claim. Distinguish recorded outcomes, live actions and proposed capabilities; quotation coverage is not implementation coverage.
shared.reuse: Reuse a diagram or recording when it answers the reader's question. Select the relevant moments; do not send the reader through the full regression laboratory.
shared.scope: The sheet unfolds the content proposal. Demo values come from preserved Canton runs; diagrams describe the cited production code and protocol. No ledger command runs when viewing this sheet.

branches.title: User
branches.question: What does this let me do?
branches.perspective: Alice wants to make a property proposal with her bank's approval.

pages.title: Start with Alice's goal
pages.show: The existing bank-to-property infographic: Alice, Northbank, Ben and Sofia, each with a clear role.
pages.message: A bank decision can enable a property proposal without sharing the bank's private papers.

pages.title: Follow the proposal
pages.show: Northbank approves → Alice proposes → Ben relays → Sofia receives. Each stop shows its consequence below the stable infographic.
pages.message: See who acts now, what changed and what happens next.

pages.title: Understand the ending
pages.show: The same purchase has two explicit endings in its carousel: proposal received, or financing declined and the proposal blocked.
pages.message: An approval enables the next action; a refusal cannot be treated as an approval.

branches.finish: I understand the journey and can recognize its outcome.

branches.title: Investor
branches.question: Show me what Harmonia makes possible on Canton.
branches.perspective: For Canton ecosystem builders and technical investors: a Keynote-style demonstration, with one model, action and observable consequence per scene.

pages.title: A private decision. A shared next step.
pages.message: Can Alice continue without receiving Northbank’s private application?
pages.show: Establish three participant nodes on one local synchronizer. Try the buyer’s forbidden action, approve as the bank, then continue as Alice. Inspect each party’s view.

demo.model: Northbank, Alice and Olivia are distinct parties, each on its own participant. Shared progress begins waiting.
demo.explain: The private application stays with Northbank. Daml restricts approval to the bank and continuation to the owner; a scoped result bridges those actions.

pages.title: An existing application. The same core.
pages.message: Can an unchanged Daml application join the workflow through a compiled adapter?
pages.show: Show the source package, its generated binding and the common StepAction interface. Compare Alice’s refused attempt with the bank’s successful action through the binding.

demo.model: One participant hosts separate party identities. A compiled adapter wraps the source application; the workflow holds a StepAction contract.
demo.explain: The source choice still enforces its authority. This is the recorded generated-adapter example, not a claim that every DAR can be integrated.

pages.title: Four parties. One final settlement.
pages.message: What commits together after all four parties are ready?
pages.show: Establish seller, buyer and two custodians on four participants. Inspect the ready state, submit settlement, then attempt it again. Keep locked and received quantities visible.

demo.model: Four participant nodes share one local synchronizer. The source has locked 10 TEST and the destination has prepared its receiving permit.
demo.explain: The eligible Settle choice performs withdrawal, receipt and trade replacement in one update. Earlier consent and preparation were separate transactions.

branches.finish: I can explain and demonstrate the Canton mechanism, including its authority and transaction boundaries.

presentation.engagement: Ask the audience to predict the outcome before revealing each recorded result. Keep the model visible.

branches.title: Architecture
branches.question: Which boundaries, dependencies and invariants make this work?
branches.perspective: For senior engineers: six inspectable diagrams, with explicit meanings for nodes, arrows and transaction boundaries.

pages.title: Deployment and dependencies
pages.message: Runtime connections and compile-time imports are different relationships.
pages.show: First locate the Scala service, participant nodes and synchronizer components. Then inspect the Daml package imports; arrows point toward dependencies.

pages.title: Submission and observation
pages.message: Follow one request through the Ledger API, then distinguish commitment, rejection and an unconfirmed result.
pages.show: The sequence shows HTTP acceptance separately from ledger completion. The state diagram explains why a transport failure requires reconciliation rather than an assumed rejection.

pages.title: Privacy and atomicity
pages.message: A scoped result connects two authorized updates; one final settlement encloses its custody operations.
pages.show: Trace issuer, consumer and continuation checks through proof consumption. Separately inspect the exact Settle transaction boundary after staged consent.

branches.finish: I can trace deployment, imports, execution, visibility and atomicity back to their production owners.

presentation.imagery: Native vector diagrams are the primary material; no decorative scenes or UI screenshots.

branches.title: Implementation
branches.question: Does the production code make sense?
branches.perspective: For Miguel’s code review: production files, their responsibilities and the real execution path.

pages.title: Find the production owners
pages.message: One financing slice: screen, shared types, service and ledger contracts.
pages.show: Read each file’s responsibility, then follow the financing slice into its types, application choice and observed result.

files.purpose: Define the shared actions and state.
Authorize the bank and create its result.

pages.title: Read the action and its authority
pages.message: Scala selects the operation; the private Daml application owns approval.
pages.show: Read the production Financing.select function beside the matching PrivateFinancing.Approve choice. Both excerpts are taken directly from the repository.

pages.title: Read the IO boundary and the result
pages.message: The service preserves uncertainty and exposes only observed participant state.
pages.show: Inspect SubmitChoice’s IO result classification, followed by the projection that derives eligible actions and displayed state from visible contracts.

branches.finish: I can review the production feature from its typed input to Daml authority and observed output.

presentation.include: Only product source needed to understand the feature.
